Content Overlap
Tags: courses,programs,specializations
Short Description: Proposers should review existing curricula and ensure that proposed courses, programs, and specializations do not contain substantial content overlap.
Content Overlap
Proposed courses, programs, and specializations are reviewed for potential content overlap with existing curricula. Proposers should review existing curricula and ensure that proposed courses, programs, and specializations do not contain substantial actual or perceived content overlap.
Early consultation with potentially affected academic units may help identify concerns, clarify distinctions between offerings, and support an efficient review process.
A letter of support, which may be provided as an email from an affected department chair, can be uploaded to the Kuali proposal to document (a) that both departments have considered potential content overlap; (b) communication between the affected department and the department proposing the curriculum; and (c) the affected department’s support for the proposed curriculum.

Modality
Tags: courses,programs,specializations
Short Description: Identifies how a curricular offering is delivered, including in-person, online, or a combination of in-person and online instruction.
Modality
Modality identifies the method of delivery for a curricular offering, including courses, programs, and specializations. It describes whether instruction occurs in person, online, or through a combination of in-person and online instruction.
The University recognizes the following modalities:

In Person
Instruction occurs at a specified physical location on specified days and times. Less than 25% of instruction is delivered online.
In Person & Online Asynchronous
Instruction combines in-person meetings on specified days and times with online asynchronous instruction. The schedule of instruction and weekly time commitment for online asynchronous instruction must be clear to students in the syllabus on the first day of class. Neither modality may account for less than 25% of total instructional time.
In Person & Online Synchronous
Instruction combines in-person and online meetings on specified days and times. Neither modality may account for less than 25% of total instructional time.

Online Synchronous
All instruction occurs online at specified days and times.
Online Synchronous & Asynchronous
All instruction occurs online and combines synchronous meetings on specified days and times with asynchronous instruction. The schedule of instruction and weekly time commitment for online asynchronous instruction must be clear to students in the syllabus. Neither modality may account for less than 25% of total instructional time.
Online Asynchronous
All instruction occurs online with no required synchronous meetings at specified days and times, except for optional online office hours or meetings. The weekly time commitment for online asynchronous instruction must be clear to students in the syllabus.
See University Manual 8.30.30

Choosing the Right Proposal Type
Choosing the Right Proposal Type
Course Proposal Types
There are two types of curricular proposals: modifying an existing curricular item or creating a new one. Selecting the correct proposal type is important. Proposals submitted under the wrong category will be denied and must be resubmitted.
Course modifications that are sometimes mistaken for new courses include:
Making a temporary course permanent
Changing the subject code of an existing course
Adding a new cross-listing to an existing course
A new course proposal is appropriate for:
Creating a new permanent course
Creating a new temporary course
Program Proposal Types
There are two types of curricular proposals: modifying an existing curricular item or creating a new one. It is important to select the correct proposal type, as proposals submitted under the wrong category will be denied and must be resubmitted.

In addition to selecting the appropriate proposal type, each program is classified under one of four credential types: Degree, Major, Certificate, or Minor. The credential type identifies the type of academic program being proposed.
Degree
An academic credential awarded by the University upon successful completion of a prescribed program of study. Degrees include bachelor’s, master’s, and doctoral degrees.
In Kuali, select Degree when the program is the only program offered under that degree. Examples include the MPS (Master of Professional Studies), BIS (Bachelor of Interdisciplinary Studies), Pharm.D. (Doctor of Pharmacy), and DNP (Doctor of Nursing Practice).
Major
A defined field of study within a degree program consisting of a required set of courses and related academic requirements in a specific discipline.
In Kuali, select Major when the program is one of multiple options offered under the same degree. These typically include BA, BS, MA, MS, and PhD programs.
Certificate
A formal program of study consisting of a defined set of courses in a focused area. Certificates may be completed independently or in conjunction with a degree program.
Minor

A secondary field of study consisting of a prescribed set of courses in a discipline outside a student’s major. A minor is intended to complement a student’s primary area of study.
Specialization Proposal Types
There are two types of curricular proposals: modifying an existing curricular item or creating a new one. It is important to select the correct proposal type, as proposals submitted under the wrong category will be denied and must be resubmitted.
At URI, these terms refer to different curricular structures. Understanding how they differ is essential to ensure that programs and their areas of study are proposed and documented correctly.

These represent a formally recognized area of study within a program. They:
Are coded in eCampus
Have defined requirements that students must complete
Appear on the student’s transcript
Are formally created and maintained through the Specializations section of Kuali
Note: The terminology used may vary by system or University Manual terminology. For curricular proposal purposes, these structures are treated as specializations in Kuali.

These represent an optional area of study within a program. They:
Are not coded in eCampus
May include suggested courses or course sequences to guide students
Do not appear on the student’s transcript
Are described within the program description to which they belong
Do not require a separate curricular proposal

Both Accelerated Bachelor’s to Master’s (ABM) programs and “4 + 1” programs are formally recognized Specializations, but they differ in how they are structured and which degree program they belong to.
ABM Specializations
Are inherited by the Master’s degree
Identify a defined pathway from the Bachelor’s degree into the Master’s degree
Include an identified set of courses that may be double-counted toward both the Bachelor’s and Master’s degree requirements
“4 + 1” Specializations
Are inherited by the Bachelor’s degree
Do not include courses that are double-counted toward both degrees
Provide guidance on courses students should take during the final semesters of their undergraduate degree to help shorten the time needed to complete the Master’s degree

Short Description: Undergraduate students must complete at least 3 credits addressing each of the 12 General Education Student Learning Outcomes, organized across four areas: Knowledge, Competencies, Responsibilities, and Integrate & Apply.
General Education Outcomes

The General Education program will assess student exposure to twelve Student Learning Outcomes in four areas:
A. Build knowledge of diverse peoples and cultures and of the natural and physical world.
(A1) STEM Disciplines (A2) Social & Behavioral Sciences (A3) Humanities (A4) Art & Design
B. Develop intellectual and interdisciplinary competencies for academic and lifelong learning.
(B1) Write Effectively (B2) Communicate Effectively (B3) Mathematical, Statistical, or Computational Strategies (B4) Information Literacy
C. Exercise individual and social responsibilities.
(C1) Civic Knowledge & Responsibilies (C2) Global Responsibility (C3) Diversity & Inclusion
D. Integrate and apply these abilities and capacities, adapting them to new settings, questions, and responsibilities to lay the foundation for lifelong learning.
(D1) Integrate & Apply

General Education courses may assess one or two Student Learning Outcomes in the following configurations:
Knowledge (A) and Competency (B)
Knowledge (A) and Responsibility (C)
Competency (B) and Competency (B)
Competency (B) and Responsibility (C)
Integration (D) and Competency (B)
Integration (D) and Responsibility (C)

Bachelor Degree Requirements
Tags: programs
Short Description: The university-wide academic and residency requirements students must meet to earn a bachelor’s degree from URI.
Bachelor Degree Requirements

Complete of a minimum of 120 credits (some majors require more)
Earn a minimum overall grade point average of 2.00 (some majors require a higher overall GPA)
Complete the coursework and other requirements for the curriculum of the major with the minimum grades per course and overall grade point averages for that major, or portions of that major, as specified in the section of the catalog which describes the requirements for each major
Complete General Education requirements, as specified elsewhere in this catalog
Abide by community standards as defined in the University Manual and Student Handbook
Complete the senior year in residence at URI
Earn one half of the total number of credits needed in the major at URI (same for a minor, if one is being pursued)
Transfer no more than half of the credits required for graduation from a two-year institution
Earn at least one-fourth of the credits required for graduation in-residence at URI (usually at least 30 credits)*
Students should review all major/degree requirements with their academic advisor to ensure completion of all course, credit and GPA minimums.
